newsitem.title: UK: IRA wounds policeman on Easter anniversary.
newsitem.headline: IRA wounds policeman on Easter anniversary.

text.p: A Northern Ireland policeman was recovering from an IRA sniper's bullet on Sunday as Irish republicans observed the 1916 anniversary of the Easter uprising against British rule, police said.
The policeman was in a serious but stable condition after being hit in the leg by a single bullet as he patrolled the village for Forkhill in the border county of Armagh.
On the other side of the border, Irish police said they had uncovered an IRA training camp including an underground firing range in the village of Scotstown in County Monaghan.
The camp was found in a three-week-old search of the border area for arms dumps used by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) in its 28-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland.
Irish republicans marked the anniversary of the Easter uprising in Dublin which hastened the end of British rule with parades and rallies across the island of Ireland.
Northern Ireland's police chief, Ronnie Flanagan, said that resurgent IRA violence had created "a very dangerous situation" in the province.

Chief Constable Ronnie Flanagan dismissed media suggestions that the Irish Republican Army was engaged in shadow boxing in the runup to British elections on May 1 and said the guerrillas were mounting "real attacks with a determination to kill."

Flanagan was speaking to Sky television the day after security forces found a 1,000-lb (500 kg) bomb abandoned in a country road where it was being assembled to ambush British soldiers from the nearby Ballykinler army base.
Superintendent Sam Martin said nine plastic bags of fertiliser-based explosive and detonators were being put together in an attempt to cause "appalling injury or death to passers-by."

No-one claimed responsibility for the device but it was thought to be the latest attempted attack on British targets of the IRA in defiance of appeals by Britain, Ireland and the United States to declare a new ceasefire.

Labour's spokeswoman on Northern Ireland, Mo Mowlam, told the British Broadasting Corporation that a truce called now would allow sufficient time to elapse for the authorities to determine it was genuine and allow Sinn Fein to the talks.
Her words appeared to signal no change in the policy adopted by Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government but a Sinn Fein spokesman said Mowlam's comments were "encouraging."

Sinn Fein's ideological foes, Protestant-backed Unionist parties which want the province to stay British, say they do not believe the IRA will call a complete halt to violence unless it is guaranteed to get the united Ireland it wants.
Peter Robinson, deputy leader of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said that if Sinn Fein were admitted to the talks, his party would walk out.

Security sources say they believe the IRA is determined to mount what they call "spectacular" attacks in advance of the May 1 election to force the next government to ease conditions for Sinn Fein to take part in the talks.
